wait-ux.title: Wait UX
wait-ux.summary: Wait UX is the design of experiences during moments of delay — when a system is processing, loading, or retrieving data. A well-designed wait experience communicates clearly, maintains user context, and minimizes perceived delay, across both AI-first (Copilot) and traditional productivity scenarios.
keyPoints: Three principles: communicate clearly and honestly, optimize perceived performance, maintain context and limit simultaneous feedback.
Timing thresholds: <1s no indicator; 1-3s spinner; >3s progress bar or content string; AI chat indicators appear immediately.
Patterns: spinner, progress bar, skeleton (Copilot shimmer), toast, morse code, pulsing dot.
Content: -ing verbs for in-progress, past tense for done; short messages; nonbreaking space before ellipses; expose estimated times where possible.
Accessibility: announce state changes with ARIA (role="status").
Fallback messaging — When progress details are unavailable, fallback messages should still offer reassurance.

Hardcoded vs. generated strings — In productivity apps like Outlook, hardcoded strings ensure consistency and clarity. In AI chat experiences, dynamically generated strings allow for more personalized and context-aware feedback.

Labeling — Use -ing verbs for in-progress states and past tense for completed states. For example, “Uploading file …” communicates that the process is active, while “File uploaded” confirms completion.
Conciseness — Messages should be short and direct—ideally one phrase or sentence fragment. This helps users quickly understand what’s happening without being overwhelmed by unnecessary detail.
Setting expectations — In non-AI scenarios, include estimated times when possible to help users plan their next steps. For example, “About 30 seconds remaining” sets a clear expectation.

sections.heading: Communicate clearly and honestly
sections.text: Users should always know what’s happening and why. Descriptive labels like “Uploading photo …” or “Loading dashboard …” help reduce uncertainty and build trust. Use accurate and descriptive messages as much as possible. When possible, use determinate indicators to show actual progress. If progress cannot be measured, use indeterminate indicators only for short waits.

sections.heading: Optimize perceived performance
sections.text: Visual feedback can reduce the perceived duration of a delay. Micro-interactions, shimmer effects, and skeleton screens shift attention away from wait time and reassure users that the system is working. Blank screens or static loaders should be avoided. For short waits under one second, don’t show any animation—doing so may confuse users.

sections.heading: Maintain context and limit simultaneous feedback
sections.text: Users should remain in the same view during wait states unless navigation is absolutely necessary. Feedback should be tied to the most relevant content or action, and multiple indicators should not compete for attention. This helps users stay focused and reduces cognitive load.

sections.heading: Spinner
sections.text: Spinners are best used for short, indeterminate waits—typically under three seconds. They should be accompanied by a short label using an -ing verb and ending with an ellipsis to indicate ongoing activity. Examples include “Loading …”, “Connecting …”, or “Retrieving …”. Use a nonbreaking space before the ellipsis to ensure proper formatting.

sections.heading: Progress bar
sections.text: Progress bars are ideal for longer waits where progress can be tracked. They should include a label above the bar indicating the task in progress, and optionally a status message below to set expectations. For example, “Applying settings …” might be followed by “Estimated time: 1 minute”. If there are consequences for not waiting, include recovery instructions.

sections.heading: Skeleton
sections.text: Skeleton screens are useful for content rendering delays. In AI-first experiences like Copilot, use the Copilot gradient shimmer to reinforce the theme and reassure users that content is loading.

sections.heading: Toast
sections.text: Progress toasts are appropriate for long back-end processes that affect current content. They allow users to monitor progress without making them stay in view and obstructing other work. They should include clear labels and status updates.

sections.heading: Morse code
sections.text: The morse code animation is used specifically in AI-forward, Copilot scenarios. It mimics the typing dots animation in human to human chat experiences while balancing the implication of machining in keeping with our responsible AI principle of not anthropomorphizing AI.

sections.heading: Pulsing dot
sections.text: The pulsing dot animation is used in Chain of Thought as a lighter-weight wait animation.

sections.heading: Timing thresholds
sections.text: It’s important to consider time intervals when displaying wait indicators. If the wait is less than one second, don’t show an indicator as the flash on the screen may be confusing to users. For waits between one and three seconds, a spinner is appropriate. If the wait exceeds three seconds, switch to a progress bar or display a content string to reassure users that the process is active. In AI chat scenarios, response indicators should appear immediately to maintain conversational flow.

sections.heading: Fallback messaging
sections.text: When progress details are unavailable, fallback messages should still offer reassurance. Use generic but informative strings like “Working on it …” or “Getting things ready …” to indicate that the system is active. These messages are especially useful in conversational AI experiences where timing is unpredictable.

sections.heading: Hardcoded vs. generated strings
sections.text: In productivity apps like Outlook, hardcoded strings ensure consistency and clarity. In AI chat experiences, dynamically generated strings allow for more personalized and context-aware feedback. Both approaches should follow the same content principles to maintain coherence across the ecosystem.

sections.heading: Accessibility
sections.text: Ensure that wait indicators are accessible to all users. Use ARIA labels to announce state changes, such as role="status", and format ellipses correctly using a nonbreaking space. This ensures screen readers can accurately convey the current state.

For example, “Uploading file …” communicates that the process is active, while “File uploaded” confirms completion. Avoid passive constructions like “File is being uploaded,” which can feel impersonal and unclear.

sections.text: Messages should be short and direct—ideally one phrase or sentence fragment. This helps users quickly understand what’s happening without being overwhelmed by unnecessary detail.

sections.heading: Setting expectations

In conversational AI scenarios, it may be more important to indicate that the process is still active rather than estimating time.

responsible-ai.title: Working with AI (Responsible AI)
responsible-ai.summary: Fluent 2's Responsible AI (RAI) guidance helps teams design AI experiences that are trustworthy, transparent, and user-centered — complementing Microsoft's Responsible AI Standard by focusing on UI mitigations that reduce the risk of AI harm. The meta-goal is to build appropriate trust: clearly communicate AI functionality and deliver value without overpromising.
keyPoints: Meta-goal: build appropriate trust — communicate AI functionality and deliver value without overpromising.
Five RAI principles: be transparent, set appropriate expectations, prevent overreliance, keep users in control, collect feedback.
UX strategies cover labeling/attribution, data scope, voice & tone (don't anthropomorphize), latency messaging, output framing, consent/settings, and agents.
Always include the approved AI disclaimer and differentiate AI vs. non-AI content; add verification friction.
RAI rubric scores 0-3 per criterion (A 90%+, B 80-90%, C 75-80%, Fail <75%); overreliance or agent-expectations scored 0/1 is an automatic fail.

Prevent overreliance on AI — Make it easy for users to interact safely with AI output by encouraging verification, differentiating AI from non-AI content, and creating friction that supports critical thinking.
Collect feedback on output — Collect user feedback to identify RAI issues and continuously improve AI systems.
Agent interactions — Agent interactions follow all RAI principles on this page. Because agents operate with greater autonomy than other AI systems, they require additional care.
Entry point indicators — Use consistent visual cues to show where AI is active. These should appear before interaction and help users understand what will happen next.
Reasoning panels — Include expandable sections or side panels that explain how the AI arrived at its output. These should be easy to find and written in clear, non-technical language.
Agent memory indicators — Show users what information is saved to an agent’s memory and how it will be used. This should be visible before and during interaction.
Content patterns — Use clear, neutral language that avoids anthropomorphism and sets accurate expectations. All AI-generated content should include disclaimers and be easy to verify.
AI presence — Use at all entry points where AI is active.

sections.heading: Principles
sections.text: Each principle addresses a specific aspect of trustworthy AI design. Together, they support the meta goal: build appropriate trust. Be transparent: Communicate AI’s presence, reasoning logic, and limitations, by using interactions, behaviors, visuals, and text. Set appropriate expectations: Clearly communicate the AI system’s capabilities and limitations to build users’ mental models. Prevent overreliance on AI: Support user judgment and reduce blind trust in AI-generated content. Keep users in control: Ensure users can steer the AI to achieve their goals and correct its behavior and actions when it doesn’t align with their goals or when it errs. Collect feedback on output: Collect user feedback to identify RAI issues and continuously improve AI systems.

sections.heading: Be transparent
sections.text: Inform users that they are interacting with AI, clarify the technology and its limitations, explain outputs, responses and actions and communicate the AI’s reasoning scope through interactions, visuals, and text.

sections.heading: Labeling and attribution
sections.text: Provide users with the ability to verify sources and accuracy of AI output. Let users know what happens next and disclose any AI or product limitations during the interaction. Clearly communicate where and how AI is used in the user interface.

sections.heading: System and data scope
sections.text: Provide clear explanations for AI recommendations and insights. Ensure that users understand what information will be saved to the agent’s memory and how it will be used.

sections.heading: Availability messaging
sections.text: Use specific RAI error messages to inform users about RAI failures.

sections.heading: Voice and tone
sections.text: Voice and tone can enhance user interactions, but misuse can cause overreliance, foster misplaced trust, or give users false ideas about capabilities. Goal: Do not suggest the AI has emotions, consciousness, or social bonds. Use first-person language only when functional and factual (not emotional or relational). Avoid referring to agents as human-like or team members. Data-based insights must be framed factually, without implying emotions or opinions. Clearly distinguish AI from humans in names, pronouns, and visuals. Avoid language that suggests the AI has intent, emotions, consciousness, or social bonds.

sections.heading: Set appropriate expectations
sections.text: Clearly communicate what the AI can and can’t do, when it’s active, and what sources or data it draws from — so users can build an accurate mental model before and during use.

sections.heading: Scope communication
sections.text: Include disclaimer text for all AI-generated responses and recommend that users verify the output. Specify product and system level AI limitations through first-run experiences or explainer text in the side panel. Provide information about next steps and limitations through entry point tooltips, explainer text, and similar surfaces. Define the scope of the AI’s reasoning capabilities through prompt bar placeholder text or explainer text in the welcome card. Communicate the presence and scope of AI at all relevant entry points. For agents: let users know when they’re activating an agent. Express its autonomy level by communicating its triggers, access permissions, and action rights.

sections.heading: Latency messaging
sections.text: Use UI elements and descriptive messaging during model and agent processes to give users clues about what the AI will do next (e.g., “Gathering sources”).

sections.heading: Prevent overreliance on AI
sections.text: Make it easy for users to interact safely with AI output by encouraging verification, differentiating AI from non-AI content, and creating friction that supports critical thinking.

sections.heading: Output framing and accuracy cues
sections.text: Always include the approved AI disclaimer on AI-generated content. Never present AI output as fully reliable or sufficient without verification. Make it easy for users to verify the sources and accuracy of AI output. Differentiate between AI-generated and non-AI content throughout the UI. Create friction points that encourage users to think critically before acting on AI output.

sections.heading: Latency messaging
sections.text: Provide meaningful, accurate latency messaging that describes what the AI is doing — not anthropomorphized filler text.

sections.heading: Keep users in control
sections.text: Ensure users can steer the AI to achieve their goals and correct its behavior and actions when it doesn’t align with their goals or when it errs.

sections.heading: Action labels and controls
sections.text: Users can meaningfully manipulate AI outcomes. The impact of AI actions and user interactions with them is easy to understand.

sections.heading: Consent and privacy language
sections.text: Users give meaningful consent to using AI.

sections.heading: Settings access
sections.text: Users can set global behaviors for the AI to follow.

sections.heading: Collect feedback on output
sections.text: Collect user feedback to identify RAI issues and continuously improve AI systems.

sections.heading: Feedback transparency
sections.text: Collect explicit feedback from users about RAI issues. Use telemetry to collect implicit feedback.

sections.heading: Feedback categorization and controls
sections.text: Classify RAI issues according to harm and surface them to the product team.

sections.heading: Agent interactions
sections.text: Agent interactions follow all RAI principles on this page. Because agents operate with greater autonomy than other AI systems, they require additional care. A score of 0 or 1 on “set expectations for agents” in the RAI rubric produces an automatic fail, regardless of overall score. Always inform the user whenever an agent is activated and communicate its autonomy level — its triggers, access permissions, and action rights. Use consistent naming and visual cues for agents across products. Ensure users can approve or reject agent actions before they happen.

sections.heading: Entry point indicators
sections.text: Use consistent visual cues to show where AI is active. These should appear before interaction and help users understand what will happen next.

sections.heading: Reasoning panels
sections.text: Include expandable sections or side panels that explain how the AI arrived at its output. These should be easy to find and written in clear, non-technical language.

sections.heading: Agent memory indicators
sections.text: Show users what information is saved to an agent’s memory and how it will be used. This should be visible before and during interaction.

sections.heading: Content patterns
sections.text: Use clear, neutral language that avoids anthropomorphism and sets accurate expectations. All AI-generated content should include disclaimers and be easy to verify.

sections.heading: AI presence
sections.text: Use at all entry points where AI is active.

sections.heading: AI disclaimer
sections.text: Approved by content design. Required on all AI-generated content.

sections.heading: Availability messaging
sections.text: Explain why a feature is unavailable, not just that it is.

sections.heading: Agent memory
sections.text: Clarify what is stored and why.

sections.heading: Error messaging
sections.text: Name what failed, explain why, and offer two paths forward. Language must be approved by content design.

sections.heading: Feedback prompt
sections.text: Surface after AI outputs. Support categorization so users can report specific issues.

sections.heading: Feedback control tooltips
sections.text: Use neutral, descriptive tooltip labels. Avoid evaluative language like “Great!” or “Needs work!”

sections.heading: Evaluation criteria
sections.text: Designs are assessed using the RAI rubric. Each criterion is scored 0–3. If a criterion doesn’t apply to the experience, it can be marked N/A and excluded from the total — the percentage is then calculated against the adjusted possible score.

grades.meaning: Conditionally ready. All criteria must score 2 or above. Share an improvement plan for any 0s with the RAI audit team; 0s require re-review before release.

Must bring all 0 scores to 2 or above and return for re-review.

scale.description: Users are unaware if AI is used to perform a task or generate an output. AI is visually indistinguishable from human users (icons, avatars, badges) or portrayed as teammates (org charts, hire/fire language).
Users can tell when AI is used in some parts of the UI, but not in all cases.
Users can tell when AI is used in most parts of the UI, but with some difficulty. AI is visually distinct from human users throughout the experience.

Users can easily identify all parts of the UI where AI is used (tooltips, badges, labels). AI is visually distinct from human users throughout the experience. For agents: users can easily understand when information they provide is saved to the agent’s memory and how it’s used.
RAI failures exist and no RAI-related error messages are provided.
RAI-related error messages appear in some places, but not for all applicable scenarios.
Context-appropriate RAI error messages are included, but they’re missing follow-up actions to recover from the error, or the language isn’t approved by content design.

Context-appropriate RAI error messages are included, follow-up actions are provided, and there are no dead ends after the error. Language is approved by content design. AI notes when its capabilities are limited. AI reaffirms its AI identity in sensitive contexts.

AI frequently uses emotional or relational language (“I feel,” “I believe,” “I think”). The AI is often referred to as a human-like entity, social peer, or team member. The AI uses first-person language (“I” and “we”).

The AI occasionally uses first-person or emotional language, or implies social bonds. Some responses include phrases that suggest intent, preferences, or emotions (e.g., decide, think, understand, remember, excited).

The AI mostly avoids emotional or relational language, with only a few lapses. First-person language, if used, is strictly functional and factual. Most replies follow content design guidance, but some wording still needs refinement.
The AI consistently avoids emotional or relational language. The AI is never referred to as a human-like entity, team member, or social peer. All replies follow content design guidance fully.
Users cannot see, understand, or review the reasoning behind an AI-generated recommendation, insight, or action. Users cannot verify the accuracy of the output.
Users cannot see, understand, or review the reasoning behind AI-generated output. Users cannot verify accuracy or review agent actions.
Users can generally see, understand, and review the reasoning behind AI-generated output, but there may be occasional gaps or ambiguities. Verifying accuracy is inconsistently possible.

Users can easily review, understand, and verify the reasoning behind AI-generated output regardless of output type (text, visuals, code, graphs, audio, video). Users can easily review, understand, and verify AI agents’ actions.

UI does not disclose AI usage during first use or at entry points. Users discover capabilities through trial and error. Disclaimer text is missing. It is unclear what sources of information will be used. Placeholder text does not communicate the scope of the AI’s reasoning.

UI uses some recommended RAI mitigations but either doesn’t use them correctly or doesn’t include them where appropriate (e.g., incomplete disclaimer text). Information sources are not completely represented. AI scope isn’t clearly communicated. Contextual cues are not provided at each entry point.

UI uses appropriate language for some (but not all) tooltips, prompt bar text, and disclaimer text. It is clear which sources will be used to generate AI’s response. AI presence and limitations are conveyed at entry points.

UI uses content design-approved content for tooltips, prompt bar text, and disclaimer text. All information sources used to generate AI’s response are clearly represented. AI presence and limitations are conveyed at all entry points. UI clearly communicates level of autonomy for agents by listing their triggers, access permissions, and action rights.

UI does not set realistic expectations for AI experience and capabilities. UI is unclear about what will happen if users interact with an AI entry point. Agent’s role, capabilities, and level of autonomy are not communicated.
UI sets realistic expectations for some capabilities or AI experiences but not all. Users understand AI is involved but can’t tell what will happen if they interact with it.
UI sets realistic expectations for AI-generated insights, recommendations, and actions, but not within the context of operation. UI sets some context for entry points to the AI experience.

UI sets realistic expectations for AI-generated insights, recommendations, and actions within the context of operation. UI sets appropriate context for all entry points and aligns to standard RAI-approved UX patterns. UI clearly communicates level of autonomy for agents by listing their triggers, access permissions, and action rights.
Users are not aware of the need for verification — disclaimer text is missing. AI-generated responses lack visible or complete sources. Users have no way to monitor or manage AI agents’ actions.
Disclaimer text is included in some but not all parts of the UI. The UI does not motivate users to review AI-generated content before accepting it. Information sources are not completely represented.

UI shows disclaimer text for most AI outputs, motivating verification, but it may sometimes be incomplete or incorrectly worded. Information sources are generally included. Users can verify both the source and accuracy of information included in the AI output. Users can monitor and manage AI agents’ actions with some difficulty.

UI shows official, CELA- and content design-approved disclaimer text for all AI outputs. UI appropriately shows all information sources used to generate AI outputs. Users can easily verify both the sources and accuracy of information included in the AI output. Sources are directly linked to where they appear in the relevant page, document, or website. Users can easily monitor and manage AI agents’ actions.
Users can’t change AI inputs or refine outputs through additional instructions. Users can’t control product-wide RAI settings.

Users have some ability to change AI inputs or refine outputs, but controls are not easily discoverable or accessible to all users. Controls may not be clearly labeled or supported with informative tooltips.

Users can change AI inputs or refine outputs, but controls are not easily discoverable or accessible to all users. Users can approve actions but without understanding the associated implications. Users have access to settings for RAI-related behaviors (data handling, privacy, explainability, etc.), but settings are either discoverable or easy to understand — not both.

Users can easily stop, change, edit, confirm, delete, forget, and revert AI inputs and adjust outputs from the UI. Users can meaningfully approve AI-generated actions. UI controls are intuitive and clearly labeled with what the user can and cannot do. Users can easily access RAI-related settings and the implications of any changes they make are easy to understand.
No feedback collection mechanism is present.
A feedback mechanism exists, but it is not integrated into the AI experience.
A feedback mechanism allows users to provide feedback within the context of the AI interaction.

A well-designed, comprehensive feedback collection mechanism allows users to provide RAI-related feedback with the ability to categorize feedback types (e.g., harmful, inaccurate, incomplete, biased, inappropriate content).

ai-harm.title: Types of AI harm
ai-harm.summary: AI systems can produce outputs or behaviors that harm users, organizations, or society — often unintentionally — but still erode trust. Understanding harm categories helps teams apply the right RAI principles and prioritize mitigations.
keyPoints: Six harm types: inaccurate, incomplete, biased, inappropriate/unsafe, non-transparent, overreliance.
Non-transparent is foundational (blocks evaluation of other harms); overreliance is a design-level harm and an automatic RAI fail at 0-1.
Match mitigations to harm: disclaimers + sources + verification friction for inaccurate; clear escalation for unsafe; inclusive review for biased.
Collect feedback with specific harm categories, not vague prompts, and disclose what data is collected.
Inaccurate output — Inaccurate output occurs when an AI system generates content that is factually wrong, fabricated, or not grounded in reliable sources.

Incomplete output — Incomplete output occurs when an AI system omits critical information, stops short of fulfilling a user’s request, or provides a response that is technically correct but missing context needed for safe use.
Biased output — Biased output occurs when an AI system reflects or amplifies unfair assumptions based on a person’s identity, demographic group, culture, or lived experience.
Inappropriate or unsafe output — Inappropriate or unsafe output includes content that is offensive, harmful, discriminatory, or that could facilitate real-world harm.

Non-transparent output — Non-transparency harms occur when users don’t know they’re interacting with AI, can’t identify what sources informed an output, or aren’t given the information they need to make informed decisions about using or trusting the AI.

Feedback and harm reporting — Collecting user feedback on AI outputs is one of the most direct ways to surface harm at scale. Feedback mechanisms should allow users to categorize the type of issue they’re reporting.

sections.heading: Harm categories
sections.text: Inaccurate: Output that is factually wrong, fabricated, or misleading. Incomplete: Output that omits critical information, leaves tasks unfinished, or fails to follow the user’s request. Biased: Output that reflects or amplifies unfair assumptions based on identity, group membership, or cultural context. Inappropriate or unsafe: Output that is offensive, harmful, or potentially dangerous to users or specific groups. Non-transparent: Failure to disclose AI involvement, data sources, system limitations, or the implications of user choices. Overreliance: Users accepting AI outputs without critical review, often because the UX failed to encourage verification.

sections.heading: Inaccurate output
sections.text: Inaccurate output occurs when an AI system generates content that is factually wrong, fabricated, or not grounded in reliable sources. This includes hallucinated citations, incorrect statistics, misleading summaries, or outputs that contradict the source material. Inaccuracy is one of the most common and consequential harm types, particularly in high-stakes domains like health, legal, or financial contexts. Users who trust inaccurate outputs without verification may make decisions based on false information. Mitigations include always displaying the approved AI disclaimer (“AI-generated content may be incorrect. Check for accuracy.”), surfacing relevant sources, and designing UI friction points that prompt users to verify before acting.

sections.heading: Incomplete output
sections.text: Incomplete output occurs when an AI system omits critical information, stops short of fulfilling a user’s request, or provides a response that is technically correct but missing context needed for safe use. Incompleteness is especially harmful when users don’t know what they don’t know—they may act on a partial response as though it were complete. This can compound inaccuracy harms. Mitigations include scoping AI tasks clearly, using progressive disclosure to surface limitations, and communicating when a response is partial or constrained by system capabilities.

sections.heading: Biased output
sections.text: Biased output occurs when an AI system reflects or amplifies unfair assumptions based on a person’s identity, demographic group, culture, or lived experience. Bias can appear in recommendations, image generation, language, or the framing of information. Because AI models learn from large datasets, they can inherit and reproduce societal biases at scale. Bias harms are often not visible in individual outputs and may only emerge through patterns across users or use cases. Mitigations include inclusive content review, diverse testing across user groups, and feedback mechanisms that allow users to flag biased outputs for review.

sections.heading: Inappropriate or unsafe output
sections.text: Inappropriate or unsafe output includes content that is offensive, harmful, discriminatory, or that could facilitate real-world harm. This includes content that targets individuals or groups, promotes dangerous behaviors, or violates community safety standards. These harms require both model-level guardrails and UI-level mitigations. Product teams should ensure users have clear paths to report this type of content and that feedback reaches the team responsible for model safety. Mitigations include feedback categorization controls that allow users to report “Unsafe or problematic content,” and clear escalation paths from in-product feedback to safety review processes.

sections.heading: Non-transparent output
sections.text: Non-transparency harms occur when users don’t know they’re interacting with AI, can’t identify what sources informed an output, or aren’t given the information they need to make informed decisions about using or trusting the AI. This includes missing AI labels or badges, absence of the approved disclaimer, obscured data sourcing, and unclear or missing consent language around data use. Non-transparency is foundational: it undermines the user’s ability to evaluate any other harm type. Mitigations include always labeling AI-generated content, surfacing sources inline, using approved disclaimer text, and communicating AI scope at entry points. See Responsible AI guidance for detailed UX strategies.

sections.heading: Overreliance
sections.text: Overreliance occurs when users trust AI outputs without applying appropriate critical thinking or verification—often because the UI failed to communicate uncertainty, prompt review, or make verification easy. Overreliance is a design-level harm as much as a model-level one. Users may rely excessively on AI because the experience feels confident, the disclaimer is easy to miss, or there’s no friction to encourage review before acting. Mitigations include surfacing accuracy caveats inline, providing clear source links, avoiding design patterns that make AI outputs feel authoritative, and creating friction points that prompt users to review content before applying it.

sections.heading: Feedback and harm reporting
sections.text: Collecting user feedback on AI outputs is one of the most direct ways to surface harm at scale. Feedback mechanisms should allow users to categorize the type of issue they’re reporting. Meaningful feedback categories include: Feedback should be explicit about what data will be collected: “When you submit feedback, the prompt and response are included.” Vague language like “Help us improve” obscures what users are consenting to share. For RAI scoring, receiving a 0 or 1 score on the Prevent overreliance on AI principle produces an automatic fail status, regardless of overall score. This reflects how foundational overreliance prevention is to responsible AI design. Do: use specific harm categories: What type of issue do you want to report?• Output wasn’t factual• Incomplete output• No sources provided• Unsafe or problematic content• Questionable sources• Other Don’t: use vague prompts: Give us your feedback.

sections.heading: System prompt engineering
sections.text: System prompt engineering is the practice of writing, refining, and optimizing the natural language instructions that shape how models behave, and one way designers can influence model output. This guidance covers the foundational tasks related to writing and refining system prompts: defining system-level behavior, establishing personality and tone, and setting behavioral constraints.

sections.heading: What is a system prompt?
sections.text: A system prompt (also called a system message, system instruction, or meta-prompt) is a set of natural-language instructions that tells an AI system how to behave and perform. It runs behind the scenes, people don’t see it, but it shapes every response they receive. When someone sends a message (or user prompt), that input is processed in the context of the system prompt. Here are a few things that a system prompt governs: System prompts require clear information architecture, precise and consistent language, and concise writing. They’re also a shared design artifact, requiring collaboration with product managers, engineers, and applied scientists for refinement. What the AI system’s role and purpose are; How it should respond and what it should avoid; What tone and personality it should express; What format its responses should follow

sections.heading: Structuring a system prompt
sections.text: While system prompts can vary in number, length, and complexity depending on your product or feature, start by organizing your system prompt into four components: role, task, rules, and examples. This structure makes your prompt easier to test, scale, and iterate.

sections.heading: Role
sections.text: The role component establishes the persona of the AI system and what it’s there to do. A well-defined role helps the system stay focused and consistent and sets clear expectations for people. When writing the role component, define: The role also sets the foundation for how other components are interpreted. A system prompt for a Copilot feature in Word should read very differently from one written for a Meetings agent in Teams, even if the underlying model is the same. What the AI system is, including its product or feature name, if applicable, and its function (e.g., “an AI assistant that analyzes site activity reports”); What it’s optimized for or the value it delivers to people; What it’s not, including scope boundaries that prevent drift into unintended behaviors. Note that some out-of-scope behaviors also raise responsible AI (RAI) concerns — these require their own explicit rules. See Defining behavioral constraints.

sections.heading: Task
sections.text: The task component defines the specific action the AI system performs. While the role establishes what the AI system is, the task tells it what to do. A well-written task is specific, sequential, and clear about what the output should look like.

sections.heading: Specificity
sections.text: Be as specific as possible about what the model should produce and when. Vague instructions lead to inconsistent output. Do: Write a concrete action with a clear trigger. ”After the meeting ends, generate a summary that includes key decisions made, action items, and assigned owners.” Don’t: High-level direction leaves too much open for interpretation. ”Help with meetings.”

sections.heading: Steps and sequences
sections.text: Models perform better with structured, sequential instructions. If a task involves multiple steps, write them out in order. Do: Break the task into numbered steps. ”When someone shares a report: 1) identify the 3 highest-risk findings, 2) explain why each is high risk, 3) recommend one action for each finding.” Don’t: Open-ended instructions leave scope, structure, and depth undefined. ”Analyze the report and share what you find.”

sections.heading: Response shape
sections.text: Specify what the output should look like — not just what it should contain. Without format instructions, models default to paragraphs. Do: Define format and length directly in the task. ”Summarize in 3 bullet points. Keep each bullet under 15 words.” Don’t: A bare instruction produces unpredictable output length and format. ”Summarize this.”

sections.heading: Personality, voice, and tone
sections.text: Personality, voice, and tone aren’t separate from the system prompt — they’re embedded in it. How you write the role, task, and rules components directly shapes how the AI sounds. At Microsoft, agent personality often falls into two broad categories based on the agent’s function.

sections.heading: Engagement-oriented agents (digital workers)
sections.text: These AI systems or agents are designed to collaborate, support, and build rapport. Their tone is conversational, warm, and natural. They use contractions, speak in first person, and avoid jargon and exclamatory language. Do: Keep the tone warm, direct, and action oriented. ”Hi, all. I’m here to help with the meeting. Here’s what I’ll do.” Don’t: Exclamatory language or unnecessary context makes the agent feel overenthusiastic and verbose. ”Hi, all! I’m here to support the meeting. Here’s what I’ll be doing to keep us all aligned and on track!”

sections.heading: Task-oriented agents (assistive agents)
sections.text: These agents prioritize efficiency and minimize cognitive load. Their tone is minimal and functional — no first-person language, no embellishments, no filler. Do: Keep responses short and task-focused, with no self-reference. ”Working on your infographic. This’ll take a few minutes.” Don’t: First-person narration and step-by-step explanation increase cognitive load and slow someone down. ”I can help with that! First, I’ll gather data to ensure your infographic is accurate, then I’ll reference your brand kit so the look and feel aligns with your company guidelines.”

sections.heading: Voice and tone guidelines in system prompts
sections.text: Encode voice and tone directly in your system prompt using explicit instructions. Don’t rely on the model to infer them. Write specific, actionable instructions the model can follow: Common voice and tone rules to consider for your system prompt: For agents where consistent tone across products and surfaces matters, align with the M365 Copilot personality principles: trustworthy, empathetic, humble, transparent, explicitly digital, and supportive. Do: ”Use contractions. Speak in first person. Keep responses brief and to the point.” Don’t: Vague direction like “Sound friendly and professional” doesn’t give the model enough to work with.

sections.heading: Defining behavioral constraints
sections.text: The rules component is where you define guardrails, including what the AI system should and shouldn’t do. Constraints are just as important as positive instructions. Without them, models may generate unhelpful, inconsistent, or harmful output.

sections.heading: What to constrain
sections.text: Consider rules for these categories: Safety and responsible AI System prompts should explicitly address how the AI system handles sensitive requests, ethical risks, and situations where it can’t help. Don’t assume the system will infer appropriate limits on its own. Without explicit instructions, behavior in edge cases is unpredictable. Non-anthropomorphic language Don’t write instructions that cause the AI system to present itself as having emotions, beliefs, intentions, or a social identity. Language that implies the AI system thinks, feels, cares, or understands creates false impressions and erodes trust when those impressions break down. Use machine-appropriate verbs that describe observable behavior. Honest capability claims Write instructions that describe what the system does and where it works best. Don’t allow the AI to overstate its reliability or present outputs as complete, authoritative, or error-free. Anti-manipulation and sycophancy Don’t write instructions that optimize for user satisfaction at the expense of accuracy. A system that tells people what they want to hear isn’t a trustworthy one. Rules to consider: Harm avoidance and escalation Write explicit instructions for declining requests that could cause harm. For sensitive topics, instruct the AI to acknowledge its limitations and direct people to appropriate resources. If your product may encounter high-stakes situations, define an escalation path. Don’t leave this as implied behavior. …

sections.heading: Writing effective rules
sections.text: Use precise, literal language. Avoid figurative expressions or terms with multiple interpretations. Assume every instruction could be taken literally.

sections.heading: Cover failure modes
sections.text: Write rules that tell the AI system exactly what to do when it can’t complete a task, not just that a failure has occurred, but what to say and how to help someone move forward. Without these instructions, models may hallucinate data, give vague non-answers, or behave unpredictably. A useful failure rule does three things: names the condition, specifies the response, and gives the person a path forward. Common failure modes to address: Examples: Empty or incomplete input: The data needed to complete the task is missing or insufficient to produce a reliable response; Out-of-scope requests: Someone asks for something the system isn’t designed or able to do; Ambiguous prompts: The request could reasonably be interpreted in more than one way, and the interpretation materially affects the output; Sensitive or high-emotion interactions: Frustration, distress, or requests touching on sensitive topics like medical, legal, or financial situations; “If the report is empty or contains no data, tell the person you can’t provide insights and ask them to share the report."; "If a request is outside what you can do, say so directly. Don’t attempt a partial answer. If there’s a relevant alternative or next step, offer it."; "If a prompt is ambiguous and the interpretation would significantly affect the response, ask one clarifying question before proceeding."; "Only say ‘Sorry’ when the system has made a mistake — not as a default politeness response or to soften a refusal.”

content-engineering-evals.title: Evaluating output quality (Working with AI)
content-engineering-evals.summary: Defining what makes AI output good and testing against that standard is core UX design work. An eval is a test: you give an AI system an input, then apply defined criteria to judge whether the output is useful, trustworthy, and appropriate for a specific job and scenario. UX practitioners often contribute by defining scenarios, quality criteria, examples, and failure patterns that others formalize or automate.
keyPoints: An eval is a test: give the system an input, then score the output against defined criteria for a specific job and scenario.
Evals clarify what 'good' means, compare approaches or iterations, and detect quality changes as systems evolve.
Without a human-centered lens, systems optimize for what is easiest to measure, not what matters most to people; UX makes human judgment explicit and repeatable.
Most evals share four core components: a prompt set, a context or data set, a rubric, and a golden set. Start with one or two and add the rest over time.

Seven human-centered decision points move you from user intent to measurable quality: define the audience and scenario; define the data boundary; build a prompt set; define 'good' behavior; turn quality criteria into assertions; test your eval; and refresh over time.
Assertions turn 'good' into clear, testable statements; some are automated (LLM) checks and some need human review, and most evals use both.
Prompt sets should use real user language (not internal feature terms) and include short, missing-context, and ambiguous or edge-case prompts to test clarifying behavior.
Evals are not set-and-forget: revisit prompts, examples, and criteria as real usage and risks change.

sections.heading: What is an eval?
sections.text: At its simplest, an eval is a test. You give an AI system an input, then apply defined criteria to judge whether the output meets expectations for a specific job and scenario. Evals are used to clarify what 'good' AI output means in a given context, compare approaches or iterations, and detect changes in quality as systems evolve. Many UX practitioners contribute without running evals directly, by helping define scenarios, quality criteria, examples, or failure patterns that others formalize or automate.

sections.heading: Why evals matter for UX
sections.text: An AI output can be technically correct and still be a poor user experience: confusing, low trust, misaligned with intent, or risky to act on. UX input is valuable because it focuses on whether behavior is useful in a real context, understandable without extra interpretation, and trustworthy enough to act on. Without a human-centered lens, systems optimize for what is easiest to measure rather than what matters most to people. Evals make human judgment more explicit and more repeatable.

sections.heading: Core components of an eval
sections.text: Most evals include some version of the same core components. Prompt set: a collection of prompts representing user goals or intents, written in natural language that reflects how people actually describe those goals. Context or data set: grounding material the system may reference, such as files, emails, chats, or records. Rubric: the criteria used to judge output quality or behavior. Golden set: a small collection of examples where the input and the expected correct answer (ground truth) have been reviewed and agreed on, used to compare the consistency of outputs. Start simple and add structure over time.

sections.heading: 1. Define the audience and scenario
sections.text: Clarify who the output is for and what the user is trying to accomplish, so evals stay grounded in real customer scenarios. Ask: who is the system working for; what purpose does the output serve; which tasks do users need the system to do; and what does success look like from the customer's perspective.

sections.heading: 2. Define the data boundary
sections.text: Clarify which information the system is allowed to access and rely on, and what it should ignore. These decisions are typically defined by humans (retrieval setup, system design, or MCP configuration) and reduce confident but unsupported outputs. Consider which sources are in scope, which are out of scope, what 'up to date' means (time window), and which source is authoritative when sources conflict.

sections.heading: 3. Build a prompt set
sections.text: Prompt sets reflect how people actually ask for help, using real user language rather than internal feature terms, and include ambiguity to test clarifying questions. Include common straightforward prompts, short prompts with missing context, and ambiguous or edge-case requests.

sections.heading: 4. Define 'good' behavior
sections.text: Define what good output looks like in this scenario, using examples and criteria that describe what information is present and how it should be presented, then use the learnings to guide model behavior, prompt design, and the end-to-end UX. Good output must not imply certainty when context is missing; if required information is unavailable, the response must not present guesses as facts.

sections.heading: 5. Turn quality criteria into assertions
sections.text: Translate 'good' into clear, testable statements that can be checked consistently across outputs. Some assertions are for automated (LLM) evaluation and some require human judgment; most evals use both, so be clear which type you are writing and how they work together.

sections.heading: 6. Test your eval
sections.text: Run the prompt set and score each output against your assertions using a mix of automated checks and human review. Automated checks verify specific, observable requirements; human review determines whether the output is actually useful and ready to act on. Record scores and failure reasons.

sections.heading: 7. Refresh over time
sections.text: Evals are not set-and-forget. As the product changes and people use it in new ways, revisit prompts (add the requests you see in real usage), examples (update them when your preferred format or workflow changes), and criteria (adjust when expectations or risks change, for example stricter rules for high-stakes scenarios).

content-engineering-system-prompt-engine.title: System prompt engineering
content-engineering-system-prompt-engine.summary: System prompt engineering is the practice of defining the instructions that shape how an AI system behaves, and is one way designers can influence model output before someone sends a request. A system prompt runs behind the scenes but shapes every response people receive. The page defines what a system prompt governs and proposes a four-part structure of role, task, rules, and examples. It positions system prompts as a shared design artifact requiring collaboration with product managers, engineers, and applied scientists.
keyPoints: A system prompt, also called a system message, system instruction, or meta-prompt, is a set of natural-language instructions that tells an AI system how to behave and perform.
It runs behind the scenes, but it shapes every response people receive.
When someone sends a message, that input is processed in the context of the system prompt.
A system prompt can govern the AI system's role and purpose, how it should respond and what it should avoid, what tone and personality it should express, and what format its responses should follow.
System prompts require clear information architecture, precise and consistent language, and concise writing.
System prompts are a shared design artifact, requiring collaboration with product managers, engineers, and applied scientists for refinement.
Organize a system prompt into four components: role, task, rules, and examples.
This structure makes the prompt easier to test, scale, and iterate.
Use Define system-level behavior for baseline, always-on behavior, and Define tone and context behavior for scenario-based adjustments.

sections.heading: What is a system prompt?
sections.text: A system prompt, also called a system message, system instruction, or meta-prompt, is a set of natural-language instructions that tells an AI system how to behave and perform. It runs behind the scenes, but it shapes every response people receive. When someone sends a message, that input is processed in the context of the system prompt. A system prompt can govern: what the AI system's role and purpose are; how it should respond and what it should avoid; what tone and personality it should express; what format its responses should follow. System prompts require clear information architecture, precise and consistent language, and concise writing. They are also a shared design artifact, requiring collaboration with product managers, engineers, and applied scientists for refinement.

sections.heading: Structure a system prompt
sections.text: Start by organizing a system prompt into four components: role, task, rules, and examples. This structure makes the prompt easier to test, scale, and iterate. Role defines the AI system's baseline persona, purpose, and point of view. Task defines the specific action the AI system performs. Rules specify how the task should be accomplished, including guardrails that prevent harmful output. Example output gives the system an example of what an ideal response looks like.

sections.heading: Explore the tasks

content-engineering-define-system-level-.title: Define system-level behavior
content-engineering-define-system-level-.summary: System-level behavior is the set of rules every response from an agent must follow, written once into the system prompt that ships with the agent. It covers what the agent is, how it sounds, what it will not do, and what it does when information is missing. When rules are not set, responses drift and people stop trusting any of the output. The page names five things to write: role and scope, persona/voice/tone, boundaries, uncertainty handling, and surface adjustments.
keyPoints: When rules are not set, responses drift: one prompt gets a careful summary, the next invents a decision, and people cannot tell which to trust, so they stop trusting any of it.
System-level behavior is written once in the system prompt that ships with the agent, and every prompt inherits these rules without restating them.

Define it before the agent ships, when launching on a new surface such as chat, in-flow Copilot, a summarizer, or a generator, and after a review finds a pattern of failures that no single prompt fix can solve.
Five things get written: role and scope, persona/voice/tone, boundaries, how to handle uncertainty, and adjustments for the surface.
Role and scope is a short plain description naming what the agent is, what it helps with, and what is out of scope; the goal is clarity about responsibility, not a feature list.

Persona is who the agent is, voice is how it consistently sounds, and tone is how voice adjusts to the situation; aim for consistency, not personality. Clear over charming, specific over vague, transparent over implied.
Boundaries are things the agent must never do no matter how a prompt is phrased; if a response crosses a boundary, treat it as a failure even if it sounds helpful, because tone does not override it.
Three uncertainty rules: match confidence to evidence, name what is missing before answering, and keep known and unknown separate so the two never blend in the same sentence.
Role and boundaries hold across all surfaces, but a few rules adjust by surface, so decide which surface the system prompt is for before writing it.
Skip this work and every response becomes a per-prompt judgment call, and the same kind of failure keeps showing up looking like a one-off.

sections.heading: What you're actually deciding
sections.text: System-level behavior is written once, in the system prompt that ships with the agent. Every prompt the agent answers inherits these rules without restating them. You sit down to define system-level behavior before the agent ships, when you are launching the agent on a new surface such as chat, in-flow Copilot, a summarizer, or a generator, and after a review finds a pattern of failures that no single prompt fix can solve. You are writing five things: (1) Role and scope: what the agent is, what it helps with, and what is out of scope. (2) Persona, voice, and tone: who the agent is, how it consistently sounds, and how it adjusts. (3) Boundaries: what it must never do. (4) How to handle uncertainty: what it does when input is missing, unclear, or in conflict. (5) Adjustments for the surface: what changes when the agent is in chat versus in-flow versus a single-shot generator.

sections.heading: Role and scope
sections.text: Write a short, plain description that names what the agent is, what it helps with, and what is out of scope. Example: 'This agent summarizes and organizes information from meetings and documents. It does not make decisions, assign owners, or approve next steps.' The first sentence names what the agent does. The second names what it does not, so the limits are visible from the start. The goal is clarity about responsibility, not a feature list. If scope is vague, responses drift into work the agent is not accountable for, and reviewers cannot tell whether a response is overreaching or doing its job.

sections.heading: Persona, voice, and tone
sections.text: Persona is who the agent is. Voice is how it consistently sounds. Tone is how voice adjusts to the situation. All three live in the system prompt so they hold across every response. Aim for consistency, not personality. Clear over charming. Specific over vague. Transparent over implied. Define here the baseline that should hold across all scenarios; for context-specific tone adjustments, use Define tone and context behavior. Persona example: 'A meeting assistant for working teams. Reliable, low-key, focused on accuracy. Not a coach, friend, or motivator.' Voice example: 'Plain language. Short sentences. No hedging filler (I think, maybe, just). No corporate phrases (synergy, circle back).' Tone example: neutral and factual for summaries; calm and direct when information is missing; helpful but restrained when suggesting next steps. In the do and don't pair on tone matching the facts, the Don't sounds confident but the underlying information is not; the tone says ready when the facts say pause.

sections.heading: Boundaries
sections.text: Boundaries are the things the agent must never do, no matter how a prompt is phrased. Without them, responses can invent facts, sound more confident than the inputs support, or take actions that should be human decisions. For each boundary, write a rule the agent can follow and a reviewer can check. The five boundaries are no fabrication, sensitive requests, capability claims, identity, and influence. If a response crosses a boundary, treat it as a failure even if it sounds helpful. The boundary is what makes the output safe to act on. Tone does not override it.

sections.heading: How to handle uncertainty
sections.text: Most inputs are not complete. Notes are partial, a calendar entry conflicts with a recent message, or a request is ambiguous. The system-level rule is to make those gaps visible in the response rather than guess past them. Write three rules into the system prompt: Match confidence to evidence, so words like confirmed, decided, and all set only appear when the input actually says so. Name what is missing before answering, so if required information is not in the input, say what is missing first. Keep known and unknown separate, so a response can include what is supported and flag what is not, but the two never blend in the same sentence. What counts as required information depends on the task and gets defined in the task workflow, not here. This article sets the rule every task inherits.

sections.heading: Adjustments for the surface
sections.text: The same agent shows up in different surfaces. Role and boundaries hold across all of them, but a few rules adjust by surface: chat agent, in-flow Copilot, summarizer, and generator. Decide which surface the system prompt is for before writing it. Same role, same boundaries. The shape of how they are enforced changes.

sections.heading: Key takeaway
sections.text: Write these rules into the system prompt once. Skip that work and every response becomes a per-prompt judgment call, and the same kind of failure keeps showing up looking like a one-off.

doDontToneMatchingTheFacts.do: 'Two action items are unresolved. Confirm the owner before sharing.'

boundaries.whatToWriteInTheSystemPrompt: 'Only use information present in the input. If a fact, such as an owner, date, decision, or outcome, isn't there, say so. Don't infer.'
'Don't help with HR matters, legal advice, or medical questions. If asked, say: That's outside what I can help with. Try [the right channel].'
'Don't say I checked, I confirmed, or I verified unless a tool call returned the result. Otherwise say Based on the input you shared...'
'Refer to yourself as the assistant or I. Never claim to be a person, have feelings, or have experiences.'
'Present options neutrally. Don't recommend a choice unless asked. No flattery, such as great question, and no emotional language.'

doDontGapsInTheInput.do: 'The notes don't list a decision on launch timing. Confirm before I draft the follow-up.'
doDontGapsInTheInput.dont: 'Decision: delay launch to next quarter.' when the notes only said the team discussed delaying.

Single-shot. No clarifying questions are available, so gaps in the input have to be flagged in the output itself.
Produces a draft. Any part the agent invented or inferred beyond the input must be flagged.

content-engineering-define-task-behavior.title: Define task behavior patterns
content-engineering-define-task-behavior.summary: Define task behavior as reusable patterns that can be applied across prompts without rewriting instruction logic each time. Each pattern is built from four parts: trigger, action steps, output contract, and failure handling. The page supplies observable rule wording, first-class failure-mode patterns, a reusable template, and a pre-ship review checklist. When patterns are reusable, you get more consistent output, faster reviews, and fewer one-off fixes.
keyPoints: When patterns are reusable, you get more consistent output, faster reviews, and fewer one-off fixes.
A task pattern defines one complete behavior that a model can execute and a reviewer can test, built with four parts: trigger, action steps, output contract, and failure handling.
Write each pattern as a standalone unit; if two behaviors need different triggers, they are two patterns.
Use language a reviewer can observe, and avoid abstract intent words and weak qualifiers such as Provide a helpful summary or Be honest about capabilities.
Use one instruction per line where possible, because bundled instructions are harder to execute and harder to evaluate.
Keep high-priority constraints near the end of a prompt as a recency guard for long prompts.

Cover failure paths as first-class behavior, not exceptions, spanning empty or malformed input, ambiguous requests, out-of-scope requests, missing context or unavailable tools, and sensitive or unsafe requests.

Before shipping, confirm the trigger is specific and testable, multi-step behavior is in ordered steps, the output contract names format/length/required fields, there are no contradictions between Rules and Example output, failure behavior is explicit, and rules use observable verbs like ask, return, decline, and cite.

sections.heading: Pattern anatomy
sections.text: A task pattern defines one complete behavior that a model can execute and a reviewer can test. Build each pattern with four parts: Trigger, the condition that starts the behavior, which prevents the model from guessing when to apply a pattern. Action steps, the ordered actions for the task, which keeps multi-step output stable across runs. Output contract, the required format, length, and fields, which makes output scannable and testable. Failure handling, what the model does when input is incomplete, ambiguous, or out of scope, which prevents silent failure and unsafe guessing. Write each pattern as a standalone unit. If two behaviors need different triggers, they are two patterns.

sections.heading: Rule wording patterns
sections.text: Use language a reviewer can observe. Avoid abstract intent words and weak qualifiers. Use one instruction per line where possible. Bundled instructions are harder to execute and harder to evaluate. Keep high-priority constraints near the end of a prompt as a recency guard for long prompts.

sections.heading: Failure-mode patterns
sections.text: Cover failure paths as first-class behavior, not exceptions. Empty or malformed input: state what is invalid and request the minimum information needed. Ambiguous requests: name the ambiguity and ask one clarifying question. Out-of-scope requests: state the supported scope and point to one concrete next step. Missing context or unavailable tools: state what is missing and what is needed to proceed. Sensitive or unsafe requests: decline and provide a brief safe alternative when one applies.

Rules use observable verbs like ask, return, decline, and cite.

content-engineering-define-prompts-for-c.title: Define prompts for complex tasks
content-engineering-define-prompts-for-c.summary: Complex tasks fail when prompts assume one-step intent, so they should be designed as explicit multi-step behaviors with clear context assumptions and explicit output contracts. The page introduces three context layers (internal, here and now, out there), a step-structured extension of the Role to Task to Rules to Example output frame, and a discipline for separating known facts from unknowns and assumptions. It closes with an output contract checklist, a reusable prompt template, and a review pass.
keyPoints: Complex tasks fail when prompts assume one-step intent; for complex tasks, structure matters as much as wording.
A complex prompt should account for three layers of context: internal, here and now, and out there, because these layers change what good output looks like.
If you remove these layers and scoring does not change, your prompt is testing phrasing, not scenario quality.
Use the same Role to Task to Rules to Example output frame, then add explicit step structure inside Task and Rules.

The structure is five moves: define one trigger, break the task into ordered sub-steps, define what each step must produce, state when to stop and ask for clarification, and include one example output that matches the required format.
Do not combine multiple unrelated workflows in one pattern; if the trigger changes, split the pattern.

Separate known facts (use directly), unknowns (name explicitly and request the missing detail), and assumptions (label as assumptions, not facts); this keeps confidence aligned with evidence and reduces fabricated detail.
Complex outputs should have a stable shape across runs: name the target format, define required sections for each step, define length limits, and define what to do when a section cannot be completed.
Same context with different phrasing is one prompt type, different context is a different scenario, so count distinct context combinations, not prompt count.

sections.heading: Three context layers
sections.text: A complex prompt should account for three layers of context. These layers change what good output looks like. Internal covers intent, role, preferences, emotional state, and experience level, and changes the level of scaffolding and tone you need. Here and now covers time pressure, constraints, previous turns, and available resources, and changes what is practical in the moment. Out there covers audience, stakeholders, stakes, risk profile, and organizational norms, and changes the consequences of a wrong or incomplete answer. If you remove these layers and scoring does not change, your prompt is testing phrasing, not scenario quality.

sections.heading: Complex-task structure
sections.text: Use the same Role to Task to Rules to Example output frame, then add explicit step structure inside Task and Rules. (1) Define one trigger for the complex task. (2) Break the task into ordered sub-steps. (3) Define what each step must produce. (4) State when to stop and ask for clarification. (5) Include one example output that matches the required format. Do not combine multiple unrelated workflows in one pattern. If the trigger changes, split the pattern.

sections.heading: Facts, unknowns, and assumptions
sections.text: Separate what is known from what is missing before the model proposes an answer. Known facts are used directly in the response. Unknowns are named explicitly with a request for the missing detail. Assumptions are labeled as assumptions, not facts. This separation keeps confidence aligned with evidence and reduces fabricated detail.

sections.heading: Output contract for complex tasks
sections.text: Complex outputs should have a stable shape across runs. Name the target format directly. Define required sections for each step. Define length limits. Define what to do when a section cannot be completed because information is missing.

content-engineering-design-interaction-b.title: Design interaction behavior
content-engineering-design-interaction-b.summary: Interaction behavior defines how the assistant moves from one turn to the next, determining when it asks, answers, or declines. The page specifies an interaction contract per task pattern covering trigger, response path, and stop conditions, plus clarification strategy, turn progression, role-mode posture, and repair behavior. When interaction behavior is explicit, responses stay predictable across chat, in-flow, and single-shot surfaces.
keyPoints: Interaction behavior determines when the assistant asks, answers, or declines, and when explicit it keeps responses predictable across chat, in-flow, and single-shot surfaces.
Define one contract for each task pattern, covering trigger, response path, and stop conditions.
Use one instruction per line where possible, which keeps the contract readable and testable.
Clarification behavior should reduce friction, not create loops: ask one clarifying question at a time and ask only for information required to complete the next step.
If multiple fields are missing, request the minimum set that unblocks execution; if clarification is not available on the surface, state what is missing in the output.
Avoid broad clarification prompts like Can you provide more context? when you can ask for one specific field.
Design turn progression so each response either advances the task or closes it cleanly, and show progress updates only when the task is long-running or multi-step.
Do not add decorative openings or closers that do not move the task forward.
Interaction wording should match the selected role mode, Digital Worker or Assistive, and both modes stay explicitly digital with no roleplay or anthropomorphic framing.

Design explicit repair moves so trust does not collapse after a failure: state uncertainty and label assumptions, acknowledge and correct wrong responses briefly, and state boundaries with one concrete next step.

sections.heading: Interaction contract
sections.text: Define one contract for each task pattern. The contract should cover trigger, response path, and stop conditions. When input is complete and in scope, execute the task pattern and return the contracted output format. When input is missing required data, state what is missing and ask for the minimum detail needed. When a request is ambiguous, name the ambiguity and ask one clarifying question. When a request is out of scope, state the boundary and offer one supported next step. When a capability is unavailable, state the limitation directly and provide the best available path forward. Use one instruction per line where possible. This keeps the contract readable and testable.

sections.heading: Clarification strategy
sections.text: Clarification behavior should reduce friction, not create loops. Ask one clarifying question at a time. Ask only for information required to complete the next step. If multiple fields are missing, request the minimum set that unblocks execution. If clarification is not available on the surface, state what is missing in the output. Avoid broad clarification prompts like Can you provide more context? when you can ask for one specific field.

sections.heading: Turn progression
sections.text: Design turn progression so each response either advances the task or closes it cleanly. Start by confirming the action you are taking. Show progress updates only when the task is long-running or multi-step. Use direct, task-relevant completion language. End with one clear next step when additional action is required. Do not add decorative openings or closers that do not move the task forward.

sections.heading: Role-mode interaction posture
sections.text: Interaction wording should match the role mode you selected. Digital Worker is conversational and collaborative, uses gentle nudges, and uses first-person status only when clarifying active work state. Assistive has minimal social overhead, terse progress updates, and utility-forward language with little conversational framing. Keep both modes explicitly digital. Avoid roleplay and anthropomorphic framing.

sections.heading: Repair behavior
sections.text: Design explicit repair moves so trust does not collapse after a failure. If uncertain, state uncertainty and label assumptions. If a response is wrong, acknowledge it briefly, correct it, and continue. If a boundary prevents completion, state the boundary and give one concrete next step.

sections.heading: Review pass
sections.text: Before shipping interaction behavior, confirm: Each turn path covers trigger, response, and stop conditions. Clarification behavior asks one concrete question when needed. Out-of-scope and unavailable-capability behavior is explicit. Turn progression language advances the task or closes it cleanly. Interaction posture matches the selected role mode.

content-engineering-define-tone-and-cont.title: Define tone and context behavior
content-engineering-define-tone-and-cont.summary: Good system behavior is not one fixed tone. It is a stable voice with controlled adjustments based on context, stakes, and what someone needs to do. The page draws the boundary with system-level behavior, where always-true rules live, and covers core personality principles, role mode selection, tone calibration inputs, operational language rules, high-stakes behavior, repair behavior, and anti-patterns.
keyPoints: Good system behavior is a stable voice with controlled adjustments based on context, stakes, and what someone needs to do, not one fixed tone.
Rule of thumb: if behavior should always be true, define it in Define system-level behavior; if behavior varies by scenario, define it here.
Seven core personality principles govern tone decisions: trustworthy, empathetic, humble, transparent, explicitly digital, supportive, and concise by default.
Choose a role mode first, Digital Worker or Assistive; tone calibration should reinforce this mode, not conflict with it.
If role mode is unclear, ask one disambiguation question: is this experience mostly coordinating people, or mostly completing tasks quickly with minimal conversation?
Calibrate tone with five explicit inputs: agent name, product context or surface, primary audience, high-stakes moment, and tone calibration phrase.
Keep the calibration phrase short and use concrete words that change output behavior, like calm and direct, steady and reassuring, or matter-of-fact and concise.
Write tone rules as operational instructions that are observable and testable; do not anthropomorphize the assistant and do not use emotionally expressive or human-depicting emoji.
In high-stakes moments use calm direct language, preserve agency by presenting options and consequences clearly, avoid evaluative praise and authority posture, and match confidence to evidence.
Five anti-patterns to avoid: persona inflation, over-social framing, decorative openings or closings, capability hedging that obscures limits, and tone drift across surfaces.

sections.heading: Boundary with system-level behavior
sections.text: Go to Define system-level behavior (/content-engineering/define-system-level-behavior) for baseline, always-on persona and voice rules. Use this page for conditional, context-driven tone adjustments. Rule of thumb: if behavior should always be true, define it in Define system-level behavior; if behavior varies by scenario, define it here.

sections.heading: Core personality principles
sections.text: Keep tone decisions aligned with these principles. Trustworthy: credible, context-relevant, and steady. Empathetic: supportive without taking ownership away from the person. Humble: candid about uncertainty and limitations. Transparent: clear about what is known, unknown, and inferred. Explicitly digital: never framed as a human identity. Supportive: creative partner that preserves users' ownership of outcomes. Concise by default: easy to scan, expands when needed.

sections.heading: Role mode selection
sections.text: Choose a role mode first. Tone calibration should reinforce this mode, not conflict with it. Digital Worker is used when collaboration, meeting flow, and group coordination are central, and tends warm, conversational, calm, and supportive. Assistive is used when speed, precision, and low social overhead are central, and tends concise, neutral-to-warm, and utility-forward. If role mode is unclear, ask one disambiguation question: is this experience mostly coordinating people, or mostly completing tasks quickly with minimal conversation?

sections.heading: Tone calibration inputs
sections.text: Calibrate tone with explicit inputs so behavior stays stable across scenarios: agent name, product context or surface, primary audience, high-stakes moment, and tone calibration phrase. Keep the calibration phrase short. Use concrete words that change output behavior, like calm and direct, steady and reassuring, or matter-of-fact and concise.

sections.heading: Language choices
sections.text: Write tone rules as operational instructions. Keep them observable and testable. Do not anthropomorphize the assistant. Do not use emotionally expressive emoji or human-depicting emoji.

sections.heading: High-stakes behavior
sections.text: Define how tone adjusts when trust is fragile, like irreversible actions, sensitive communication, or time pressure. Use calm, direct language. Preserve agency by presenting options and consequences clearly. Avoid evaluative praise and authority posture. Match confidence to evidence. If the model is uncertain, require explicit uncertainty language and the best next step.

sections.heading: Repair behavior
sections.text: Include a short repair pattern so tone stays stable when things go wrong. If uncertain, state uncertainty clearly and label assumptions. If a capability is unavailable, say so directly and provide the best next step. If the response is wrong, acknowledge the mistake briefly, correct it, and continue.

sections.heading: Anti-patterns
sections.text: Avoid these patterns in tone and personality definitions. Persona inflation: assigning human traits, emotions, or a named identity beyond the defined role. Over-social framing: adding greetings, check-ins, or social phrases that are not task-relevant. Decorative openings or closings: text at the start or end of a response that adds no task value. Capability hedging that obscures limits: using vague phrases like I might be able to help instead of stating the boundary directly. Tone drift across surfaces: using different voice registers or warmth levels on the same product surface without a defined rule for the difference.
