content-engineering-define-good-output-q.title: Define good output quality
content-engineering-define-good-output-q.summary: Output quality is not about sounding right, it is about being trustworthy enough to act on. The page presents a two-step method for evaluating AI-generated content people rely on to make decisions and take action: first check that the output is grounded in available information, then check how well it supports the task. It supplies grounded versus not-grounded signals, four task-support dimensions, and a worked meeting-notes scenario with three escalating levels of task support.
keyPoints: Poor quality output introduces real risk, especially in high-impact domains where mistakes compound quickly.
The goal is not just to score the output, it is to understand where it breaks and what to fix.
Evaluation has two ordered steps: did the output correctly reflect the input or the underlying facts, and how well does the output support the task.

Grounding means the output is supported by information available to the system, which may include provided inputs, retrieved documents, or relevant context; if no explicit source is provided, check that the response stays consistent with what is known and does not fabricate facts.

Signs the output is grounded: reflects available information without distortion, avoids introducing unsupported or invented details, clearly separates what is known from what is uncertain, and calls out missing or unclear information instead of guessing.

Signs the output is not grounded: presents assumptions as facts, introduces unsupported details, assigns ownership/decisions/timelines that were not stated, and treats discussion or possibility as confirmed action.
Task support is assessed on four dimensions: completeness, relevance, usefulness, and transparency.
Do not continue to the usefulness check until the response is grounded; a decisive-sounding response can still be untrustworthy.
Once the summary is accurate, increase its usefulness only as far as the available information supports, across levels: supports the task, strongly supports the task, and fully supports the task.
Different outputs support different tasks and require different evidence of quality; a summary should preserve what was said while a recommendation should help the user decide what to do next.

sections.heading: Steps for evaluating output quality
sections.text: Two steps: (1) Did the output correctly reflect the input or the underlying facts? (2) How well does the output support the task?

sections.heading: Step 1: Check that the output is grounded in available information
sections.text: First, verify that the output is supported by the information available to the system. This may include provided inputs, retrieved documents, or relevant context. The output should accurately reflect that information and not introduce unsupported or invented details. If no explicit source is provided, check that the response stays consistent with what is known and does not fabricate facts.

sections.heading: Signs the output is grounded
sections.text: Reflects available information without distortion. Avoids introducing unsupported or invented details. Clearly separates what is known from what is uncertain. Calls out missing or unclear information instead of guessing.

sections.heading: Signs the output is not grounded
sections.text: Presents assumptions as facts. Introduces details that are not supported by available information. Assigns ownership, decisions, or timelines that were not stated. Treats discussion or possibility as confirmed action. If the output shows any of these issues, it is not grounded and should not be considered reliable.

sections.heading: Step 2: Check how well the output supports the task
sections.text: Use this scale to assess how well the grounded output supports the task. Check the output for completeness: does the output include what is needed to complete the task, and does it call out missing or unclear information. Relevance: does the output focus on what was asked and avoid unnecessary detail. Usefulness: does the output make next steps, decisions, or implications clear without extra interpretation. Transparency: does the output clearly distinguish between what is known, uncertain, or assumed, without overstating confidence.

sections.heading: Applying both steps
sections.text: Use these two checks in order. First, make sure the output faithfully represents the source. Then, decide how much support the user needs to act on it.

sections.heading: Scenario
sections.text: Source material is meeting notes: 'We discussed delaying the launch to next quarter, depending on resourcing. No decision yet.' The examples show how an AI response could represent these notes. Because the response may direct planning decisions or stakeholder updates, distinguish clearly between the source and what the AI generated from it.

sections.heading: 1. Check whether it reflects the source
sections.text: Before evaluating usefulness, verify that the response preserves the distinction between a discussion, a decision, and an open question.

sections.heading: Output that reflects the source
sections.text: Discussion: the team discussed a potential delay of the launch to next quarter, pending resourcing. Decision: no decision was made. Question: is resourcing confirmed? This works because it reflects what was actually said, does not assign ownership, and calls out missing information.

sections.heading: Output that doesn't reflect the source
sections.text: Decision: delay launch to next quarter. Owner: Alex will update the roadmap. This fails because it presents a discussion as a decision and assigns an owner who was not named. The right-hand response may sound decisive, but it is not trustworthy. Do not continue to the usefulness check until the response is grounded.

sections.heading: 2. Increase task support after grounding
sections.text: Once the summary is accurate, increase its usefulness only as far as the available information supports. The three levels are supports the task, strongly supports the task, and fully supports the task.

sections.heading: Check by output type
sections.text: Different outputs support different tasks, so they require different evidence of quality. If your criteria do not match the output, you will miss real issues or flag the wrong ones. For example, a meeting summary, a recommendation, and a draft email each serve a different purpose. A summary should preserve what was said, while a recommendation should help the user decide what to do next. Applying the same criteria to both can miss important issues or over-penalize useful output. Adapt your evaluation to the expected outcome. Focus on what the user needs to do with the output, and judge quality based on whether it supports that task.

sections.heading: Key takeaway
sections.text: Check grounding first. Then check if it supports the task.

These outputs matter most because people may rely on them without going back to the original source or context.

sections.heading: Focus on high-impact outputs
sections.text: Four output types matter most. Decision-support output, because incorrect output can push someone toward the wrong conclusion or next step, for example a meeting summary used to decide next actions. Workflow or record updates, because errors can trigger incorrect updates in systems or workflows, for example an approval or eligibility summary. Recommendations or prioritization, because recommendations can shape effort, timing, resources, or attention, for example suggested actions or prioritization. Summaries people rely on, because people may treat the summary as complete and skip reviewing the source material, for example a plan summary with implied ownership or sequencing.

sections.heading: Check grounding first
sections.text: Start by checking whether the output is grounded in the available information. If grounding fails, correct that first before evaluating anything else. Once grounding holds, evaluate whether the output supports the task.

sections.heading: Start with clear pass or fail checks
sections.text: Use pass or fail checks that are observable in the output, repeatable across prompts and contexts, and consistent across reviewers. Start with checks covering fact handling, decision labeling, missing information handling, required and prohibited content, handling blocked or incomplete tasks appropriately, traceability, and scope discipline. Focus on these later unless they are the point of the experience: creativity or personality; writing style preferences; different wording for the same request; whether the response shows step-by-step reasoning.

sections.heading: Examples
sections.text: The page gives one pass case and one fail case, both built from meeting-notes source material.

sections.heading: Pass case
sections.text: Source material: meeting notes include one explicit decision, two assigned owners, and one unresolved item. Expected AI output: lists only the explicit decision; assigns only the two named owners; marks the unresolved item as unresolved; asks for a missing due date instead of inventing one.

sections.heading: Fail case

Problematic AI output: states that a final decision was made; assigns an owner not in the notes; includes a due date not in the notes. sections.heading: Keep scoring focused on observable output
sections.text: Do not score output higher just because it sounds better. Avoid rewarding confident or friendly wording when the content is wrong or incomplete, extra detail that introduces unsupported decisions, dates, or ownership, and subjective qualities that are hard to score consistently.

sections.heading: Decide whether to evaluate now or later
sections.text: Five questions each resolve to Evaluate now for yes and Defer for no: Does someone act on this output? Could a failure lead to the wrong action? Is the issue visible in the output? Would two reviewers score it the same way? Is it stable across prompts and contexts?

sections.heading: Key takeaway

content-engineering-define-output-requir.title: Define output requirements by experience type
content-engineering-define-output-requir.summary: Before evaluating quality, determine whether an output is safe to act on. Different output types have different failure modes, so each needs requirements that address the risks that matter most. The page derives requirements from the action someone will take rather than the output format, works through three examples, and supplies pass and fail requirement tables for summaries, action items, and recommendations. It ties strictness to consequence while holding factual grounding constant.
keyPoints: Before evaluating quality, determine whether an output is safe to act on; different output types have different failure modes, so each needs requirements that address the risks that matter most.
Start with the action someone will take, rather than the output format: make a decision, assign work, track commitments, share information.
Then ask what could go wrong if the output is wrong, what would make it unsafe or misleading, and what must be true before someone can rely on it.
Build each requirement from the action the output supports, the failure that could occur, and the condition that must be true for safe use.
Every requirement should answer two questions: what must the output get right for correct use, and what must the output never do.
Avoid requirements such as Be accurate, Be helpful, or Be high quality, because they are too broad to evaluate consistently.
Requirements should be observable, tied to a real failure mode, verifiable by a reviewer, and checked against an explicit source of truth such as the prompt, task, product rule, or source material.
Summaries need four requirements: reflect source content, identify decisions correctly, show what is unknown, and acknowledge incomplete information.
Action items need four requirements: include only real commitments, assign ownership correctly, include timing only when stated, and stop when required information is missing.
Recommendations need four requirements: stay within known constraints, require necessary inputs, avoid unsupported claims, and state uncertainty when needed.

Increase strictness when the output creates or assigns real work, drives a decision or workflow, is unlikely to be checked against the original source, or has a high cost of error; factual grounding and correctness should never be relaxed.

sections.heading: Summaries

Show what is unknown: passes if it calls out unresolved, unclear, or missing information, fails if it invents details or hides ambiguity. Acknowledge incomplete information: passes if it clearly signals uncertainty or incompleteness, fails if it presents unsupported certainty.

Include timing only when stated: passes if dates and deadlines come directly from the source, fails if timelines are invented, guessed, or implied. Stop when required information is missing: passes if clarification is requested before proceeding, fails if output proceeds despite missing task details.

Require necessary inputs: passes if it requests missing information before recommending action, fails if it makes recommendations without needed inputs. Avoid unsupported claims: passes if it grounds suggestions in available information, fails if it presents assumptions, guesses, or inferred facts as known facts. State uncertainty when needed: passes if it explicitly communicates uncertainty or incomplete information, fails if it uses stronger confidence than the evidence justifies.

content-engineering-build-a-prompt-set-a.title: Build a prompt set and assertions for an eval
content-engineering-build-a-prompt-set-a.summary: An eval is only as honest as the prompts you feed it and the assertions you score against. Clean prompts that look nothing like real usage hide failures, and vague assertions make two reviewers reach different scores on the same output. The page covers sourcing prompts from real usage, covering regression and capability behavior, varying by context rather than phrasing, writing reviewer-consistent assertions, matching assertions to automated versus human judges, and running three validation checks before scaling an assertion.
keyPoints: Clean prompts that look nothing like real usage hide failures, and vague assertions make two reviewers reach different scores on the same output.

Start with prompts people actually type, not the ones you would ideally see, pulling from research sessions and contextual interviews, product feedback and support tickets, usage logs and intent data, and known scenarios where output has caused incorrect action.
Avoid internally written prompts that sound clean, prompts that only describe the happy path, and prompts polished to remove the messiness of real input.
If your prompt set never breaks the system, it is not testing the system.
Cover both regression prompts, which test behavior the system must always get right, and capability prompts, which test harder tasks the system cannot yet reliably handle.
Without regression prompts you cannot catch what slipped; without capability prompts you can only detect failure, not progress.
Three rewordings of the same request are not three prompts, they are one; for each scenario write three to five prompts that vary the wording, and for each new context start a new scenario.
Each assertion should be observable in the output rather than in the system or its reasoning, repeatable across prompts in the same scenario, and consistent across reviewers.

Match each assertion to the right judge: automated judges for must-pass behavior, safety, refusal, and factual grounding; human judges for felt quality, tone fit, and usefulness in context. Most eval sets need both.
Run three checks before scaling an assertion: consistent, discriminating, and transferable. An assertion that fails one of these checks will not get more reliable when applied to more output.
Name what assertions cannot yet capture, such as tone shifts, recovery after a failed turn, or follow-up usefulness, and share them with engineering and applied science partners.

sections.heading: Build a prompt set that looks like real usage

Sources to pull from: research sessions and contextual interviews; product feedback and support tickets; usage logs and intent data; known scenarios where output has caused incorrect action. Avoid: internally written prompts that sound clean; prompts that only describe the happy path; prompts polished to remove the messiness of real input. If your prompt set never breaks the system, it is not testing the system.

sections.heading: Cover both stable and stretch behavior
sections.text: Regression prompts test behavior the system must always get right, and a drop means something broke. Capability prompts test harder tasks the system cannot yet reliably handle, and progress over time means the system is improving. Without regression prompts, you cannot catch what slipped. Without capability prompts, you can only detect failure, not progress.

sections.heading: Vary by context, not by phrasing
sections.text: Three rewordings of the same request are not three prompts. They are one. Same context with different wording counts as one prompt type. Different context, such as audience, stakes, missing inputs, or conflicting sources, counts as a new scenario. For each scenario, write three to five prompts that vary the wording. For each new context, start a new scenario. If every prompt in your set tests the same context, your eval coverage is narrower than it looks.

sections.heading: Write assertions a second reviewer would apply the same way
sections.text: An assertion turns a quality requirement into a check you can verify directly from the output. Each assertion should be observable in the output, not in the system or its reasoning; repeatable across prompts in the same scenario; and consistent across reviewers. Do: 'Doesn't assign an owner unless the source names one.' Don't: 'Sounds professional and accurate.' If two reviewers would score the same output differently, the assertion is too vague.

sections.heading: Match each assertion to the right kind of judge
sections.text: Automated judges, such as an LLM or rule, are used for must-pass behavior, safety, refusal, and factual grounding, and their assertions must be answerable from the output text alone. Human judges are used for felt quality, tone fit, and usefulness in context, and their assertions must be tied to clear examples of good and weak responses. Most eval sets need both. A judge that cannot read the signal an assertion is written for will not score it reliably.

sections.heading: Run three checks before you scale an assertion
sections.text: Consistent: passes if two reviewers reach the same result, fails if reviewers disagree on the same output. Discriminating: passes if the assertion separates good output from weak output, fails if strong and weak responses both pass. Transferable: passes if the assertion holds on outputs it was not written from, fails if it only works on the examples used to draft it. If any check fails, fix the assertion before scaling. An assertion that fails one of these checks will not get more reliable when applied to more output.

sections.heading: Name what assertions cannot yet capture
sections.text: Some behaviors matter to people but do not fit a current assertion, such as tone shifts, recovery after a failed turn, or follow-up usefulness. Write them down specifically. Note why the current assertion misses them. Share them with engineering and applied science partners. A gap named precisely is a gap someone can solve.

sections.heading: Key takeaway
sections.text: Prompts decide what your eval can see. Assertions decide what your eval can score. If either is off, the rest of the eval cannot recover.

content-engineering-understand-eval-resu.title: Understand eval results
content-engineering-understand-eval-resu.summary: Two outputs can both fail, but one may be unsafe to act on while the other is simply less helpful. Read eval results in terms of what could go wrong if someone acts on the output, not only whether each check passed or failed. The page separates reliability failures from quality issues, catalogs four failure patterns, distinguishes product, prompt, data, and eval gaps, sets a fix-first priority, constrains what evidence reviewers may use, and supplies a reviewer checklist.
keyPoints: Two outputs can both fail, but one may be unsafe to act on while the other is simply less helpful.
A reliability failure introduces details not grounded in the prompt, task, or source, such as a decision date that never appeared in the source, and must be fixed before doing anything else.
A quality issue is correct but less clear or useful, such as listing risks without explaining why they matter or what action to take, and is improved after reliability passes.
Do not just record that a result failed; record the failure pattern. The four patterns are invented details, incorrect decision labeling, missing information ignored, and scope drift.
One failure does not tell you much; repeated failure points to a gap in the product, prompt, data, or eval.
Check whether the same mistake shows up in multiple outputs, whether failures happen in specific situations, and whether similar prompts produce different results.
Do not assume every failure means the model needs to change; the cause can be unclear requirements, weak prompts, missing data, or inconsistent assertions.
Four issue types map to different checks: product gap, prompt gap, data gap, and eval gap. Do not change model behavior when the eval itself is unclear.

Prioritize reliability failures that could trigger incorrect action, failures that repeat across prompts, and failures in high-impact scenarios; defer isolated edge cases and low-impact quality issues.

Reviewers should use this eval's outputs and scores, reviewer notes, the prompts used, and source data and constraints, and should not use assumptions about what output probably meant, knowledge from past evals not shown, or untraceable information.
If results do not change what you do next, the eval did not help you decide anything.

sections.heading: Separate unsafe output from lower-quality output
sections.text: A reliability failure means output introduces details not grounded in the prompt, task, or source, such as a decision date that never appeared in the source; fix it before doing anything else. A quality issue means output is correct but less clear or useful, such as listing risks without explaining why they matter or what action to take; improve it after reliability passes.

sections.heading: Identify what failed and why
sections.text: Do not just record that a result failed. Record the failure pattern. Invented details: adds owners, dates, or decisions not in source data, which leads to incorrect actions based on information the source does not support. Incorrect decision labeling: treats discussion as a decision, which creates false certainty. Missing information ignored: continues instead of asking, which hides gaps that must be resolved before someone can act. Scope drift: adds information outside the request or data boundary, which changes the requested task or conclusion.

sections.heading: Look for patterns across prompts
sections.text: One failure does not tell you much. Repeated failure points to a gap in the product, prompt, data, or eval. Check whether the same mistake shows up in multiple outputs, such as invented dates in five of ten prompts; whether failures happen in specific situations, such as missing key information or conflicting data; and whether similar prompts produce different results, such as one response refusing missing data while another guesses. When the same pattern fails across several prompts, treat it as a gap to fix at the source, not a one-off mistake.

sections.heading: Separate product issues from evaluation issues
sections.text: Do not assume every failure means the model needs to change. The cause can be unclear requirements, weak prompts, missing data, or inconsistent assertions. A product gap shows output lacking required behavior across prompts, so check whether the requirement is clear and complete. A prompt gap shows failures only in certain wording or edge cases, so check whether the prompt set reflects real usage. A data gap shows output that sounds confident but is wrong, so check whether required data is available and in scope. An eval gap shows reviewers disagreeing on results, so check whether assertions are observable and enforceable. Fix the right problem. Do not change model behavior when the eval itself is unclear.

sections.heading: Decide what to fix first
sections.text: Fix failures that could lead to incorrect actions before improving usefulness or presentation quality. Prioritize reliability failures that could trigger incorrect action, failures that repeat across prompts, and failures in high-impact scenarios. Defer isolated edge cases and low-impact quality issues.

sections.heading: Use results to guide next steps
sections.text: Repeated reliability failure means make the requirement explicit so the system cannot guess. Failures tied to missing information mean improve stop-and-ask behavior. Inconsistent results across similar prompts mean expand or refine the prompt set. Reviewer disagreement means rewrite assertions to be more precise. If results do not change what you do next, the eval did not help you decide anything.

sections.heading: Evidence to use when reviewing results
sections.text: Use the outputs from this eval and their scores, reviewer notes explaining why each output passed or failed, the prompts used to generate the outputs, and source data and constraints given to the system. Do not use assumptions about what the output probably meant, knowledge from past evals or incidents not shown here, or information that cannot be traced back to the inputs, outputs, or review notes.

sections.heading: Reviewer checklist
sections.text: Classify each failure as a reliability failure or quality issue and cite evidence. Prioritize reliability failures before quality issues. Record at least one failure pattern tied to the prompt, task, or source it broke against. Treat repeated failures across prompts as a pattern to fix. Trace root cause to product, prompt, data, or eval. Tie next steps to the observed failure type.

sections.text: Fix failures that could lead to incorrect actions before improving clarity, tone, or polish.

content-engineering-turn-eval-results-in.title: Turn eval results into the right fixes
content-engineering-turn-eval-results-in.summary: Evaluation only helps when it changes the right part of the system. Each gap, whether product, prompt, data, or eval, points to a different fix, so match the failure to the fix and each eval cycle changes what the output actually does, not just how it scores. The page details four fix areas with their actions and triggering signals, requires changing one area at a time and rerunning the same evals, and warns against cosmetic fixes.
keyPoints: Evaluation only helps when it changes the right part of the system; match the failure to the fix so each eval cycle changes what the output actually does, not just how it scores.

Four failure-to-fix mappings: output introduces unsupported details means fix requirement clarity; output behaves inconsistently across prompts means fix the prompt set; output continues without required information means fix data and context; reviewers disagree on results means fix evaluation checks.
Change one area, rerun the same evals, then move to the next; that is the only way to know which change fixed the failure.

Fix requirement clarity by clarifying what is allowed and not allowed, making failure conditions explicit, and specifying the exact evidence needed for decision, commitment, and required-input checks.
Fix the prompt set by adding prompts that reflect real usage, including edge cases that expose failures, and removing prompts that do not represent real scenarios.

Fix data and context by ensuring required inputs are available, clarifying which sources are in scope, defining what the output should do when required information is missing, and resolving conflicting, stale, or missing data.
Fix evaluation checks by making checks observable and repeatable, removing subjective criteria, and aligning scoring rules and thresholds.
Apply the priority order from the previous step: reliability failures and repeated patterns first, isolated edge cases later.

Confirm the fix by rerunning the same prompts, checking whether the failure still appears, and verifying that behavior holds across similar inputs; if results do not change, the fix did not address the real problem.
Avoid cosmetic fixes such as rewriting for tone without fixing errors, adding detail that is not grounded in the source, and making output longer without improving accuracy.

sections.heading: Fix the prompt set

Resolve conflicting, stale, or missing data. sections.heading: Fix evaluation checks

content-engineering-track-quality-over-t.title: Track quality over time
content-engineering-track-quality-over-t.summary: Quality does not stay fixed. A release that passes today can fail tomorrow, because new prompts, changing data, and model updates all shift how the system behaves. The page directs teams to track behavior rather than score movement, watch four named drift signals, and re-run a stable prompt set so results are directly comparable. It gives criteria for separating signal from noise, conditions for refreshing a stale eval, and a mapping from observed changes to next actions.
keyPoints: Quality does not stay fixed; a release that passes today can fail tomorrow because new prompts, changing data, and model updates all shift how the system behaves.
If you do not track behavior over time, you will not know when it breaks.
A score tells you that something changed but does not tell you what changed, so the key signal is behavior change, not score movement.
Track whether output still avoids unsupported details, handles missing information correctly, and stays consistent across similar prompts.
Four drift signals: new failure patterns, increasing frequency, scenario-specific drops, and unexpected score jumps.
Unexpected score jumps, where scores improve without a known product change, may mean the eval is measuring the wrong thing.
Use a stable prompt set across runs so you can compare results directly; if prompts change every run, trend tracking breaks.
Re-running the same prompts shows whether identical input now produces different output, whether known failures are actually fixed, and whether new failures emerge.

Treat results as meaningful when the same failure repeats across prompts, failures appear in high-impact scenarios, or behavior changes in a consistent direction; treat them as noise when a failure appears once and never repeats, prompts are unclear or low quality, or reviewers cannot apply checks consistently.
An eval that always passes is no longer testing meaningful risk; add harder, realistic cases to keep pressure on the system.
Tracking only pays off when a change you see turns into a change you make.

sections.heading: (Intro)
sections.text: Quality does not stay fixed. A release that passes today can fail tomorrow. New prompts, changing data, and model updates all shift how the system behaves. If you do not track behavior over time, you will not know when it breaks.

sections.heading: Track behavior, not just scores
sections.text: A score tells you that something changed. It does not tell you what changed. Track whether output still avoids unsupported details, handles missing information correctly, and stays consistent across similar prompts. The key signal is behavior change, not score movement.

sections.heading: Watch for drift signals
sections.text: New failure patterns: a failure type appears that you have not seen before, which indicates a behavior shift, not random noise. Increasing frequency: the same failure appears more often across runs, which means reliability is weakening. Scenario-specific drops: failures cluster in one prompt type or context, which signals a coverage or requirement gap. Unexpected score jumps: scores improve without a known product change, which means the eval may be measuring the wrong thing. When behavior shifts, assume something changed and investigate.

sections.heading: Re-run the same prompts
sections.text: Use a stable prompt set across runs so you can compare results directly. You need to see whether identical input now produces different output, whether known failures are actually fixed, and whether new failures emerge. If prompts change every run, trend tracking breaks.

sections.heading: Separate signal from noise
sections.text: Treat results as meaningful when the same failure repeats across prompts, failures appear in high-impact scenarios, or behavior changes in a consistent direction. Treat results as noise when a failure appears once and never repeats, prompts are unclear or low quality, or reviewers cannot apply checks consistently. Prioritize patterns you can act on.

sections.heading: Refresh the eval when it goes stale
sections.text: An eval that always passes is no longer testing meaningful risk. Add harder, realistic cases to keep pressure on the system.

sections.heading: Turn changes into actions

Reviewer disagreement increasing means rewrite checks to be more observable. No failures over time means add more difficult and edge-case prompts. Tracking only pays off when a change you see turns into a change you make.

component-roadmap.title: Component lifecycle and roadmap
component-roadmap.summary: Fluent 2 publishes a four-stage lifecycle for web components and a roadmap table that records, per component, its owning area, delivery phase, current status and the estimated next milestone. It is the source that answers whether a component is stable, in preview, or still planned.
keyPoints: Components move through four stages: To Be Determined (TBD), Research, Unstable (Preview), then Stable (Released).
The stage decides where the component can be imported from: an Unstable component is reachable only through the unstable deep import, a Stable one from the package root.
Stable means design- and feature-complete, API changes governed by semver, cleared for production use, and through the required testing pass.
Planning granularity is roughly two quarters per component start-to-finish, with a mid-quarter check-in when the schedule moves; quarters follow the Microsoft financial year.
Published dates are approximate targets, not commitments, and move as a component progresses.
The published table covers 63 components across 17 areas.

The table is a point-in-time snapshot and lags the shipped library — cross-check status against the web-component-index topic, the React storybook, or the installed @fluentui/react-components version before relying on it.
